doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Lincoln Center aesthetic education and composition teaching
summary: Rowe and Piltzecker bond over arts-in-education work; Piltzecker explains how Lincoln Center Institute thinking shaped his composing and teaching.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Something interesting happened this morning, and I found out afterwards and you and I shared an experience — when you got up and you were doing this little demonstration about the beat and how it can — you know you had the student between two chairs going twelve steps and then changing. Eventually the destination was the same. That exercise — when I saw you do that I said I wonder if you worked in aesthetic education — because I did and when I saw you do that I said I bet he did. And then I went up and I re- read your bios and it said indeed you worked or work for the Lincoln Center Arts in Education mode. And I did that here in Utica for many years.
Isn’t that inter — I’m so delighted that you picked up on that. And I’m thrilled that you see that and that you went back and made that connection.
Well the idea of trying to relate to get non-musicians to understand musical concepts is a wonderfully challenging endeavor I think. And it makes you think different about them I believe.

Right. The Center for Arts in Education used to be called Lincoln Center Institute years ago. And my wife, who is a modern dancer, is still working for them. She was one of the first pioneers at that, and I came in and did a few years’ work with them. But she just breathes these concepts. And I’ve learned a lot. I’ve gone to a zillion dance concerts. It’s all the same, but yes I did do that kind of work and I love it. And there was a subsidiary in Lincoln, Nebraska called the Lead Institute, the Lead Center. And they would bring us out and we would team teach. I did it also at Lincoln Center at Juilliard. But the model was you have four artists come out of theater, you know, an actor, a visual artist, a dancer and a musician, and you have this group of sixth grade teachers for two weeks. And every day you do a workshop in the morning one discipline after another discipline, and you create work. You examine works of art. You create work. You talk about these concepts. And that thinking in aesthetic education, again, it was formative for me. I didn’t realize how important it was until I really, I realized I was thinking like that the whole time, how everything is related you know, how these cross disciplines, even on the bandstand, it doesn’t matter whether it’s, and I truly believe whether it’s this jazz solo or a painter. It doesn’t make that much difference. But those concepts and thinking in large artistic parameters like gee freedom and discipline are patterns and expectations. And something stays the same and something changes and you know all those things, they’ve inspired

and in a certain sense directed a lot of my compositional thinking and sometimes my soloing too. And also it saved my tail when I became a composition professor because I wrote through a department called Studio Composition. And most of my constituents, certainly in the beginning, were singers, songwriters, rock & roll, indie bands, movie scoring people, people who write for video games you know. And so what do I know? I don’t know. I came up with — I listened to Bill Evans and Clark Terry and you know, what do I know about this stuff. But teaching in those large concepts, like somebody, to put it simply, composition is composition. It doesn’t matter. Composition is composition. And so I was able to use those concepts from the Lincoln Center Institute in order to address and hopefully contribute something meaningful to this program, rather than me being able to quote all the artists that they knew — I didn’t know them, I didn’t know them. I’m in the jazz world. My formative years were in the jazz world. But those concepts got me through and they’re still my guiding light in a lot of ways. You know and it’s old school, it’s nothing new. Thousands of years I mean, it worked for Palestrina, these things.
